title: Functions and Null Safety
subtitle: Create reusable functions and safely handle nullable values.
description: Learn function syntax, parameters, return values, default arguments, higher-order functions and Kotlin null safety.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Understand Functions and Null Safety

Welcome to Lesson 6: Functions and Null Safety. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Functions and Null Safety”. The goal is to create reusable functions and safely handle nullable values.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.

A function packages a task behind a name so callers can use it without repeating its implementation. Good functions have a focused responsibility, meaningful parameter names, and a clear result or documented side effect.

blocks.code:
fun greet(name: String): String = "Welcome, $name!"
fun main() { println(greet("Ama")) }

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates Create reusable functions and safely handle nullable values. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: A calculation is needed in three parts of the program. Which change reduces duplicated logic?
options: Copy the calculation to three new places.
Turn the result into a comment.
Create a focused function and call it with the required inputs.
Store the calculation in the page title.
blocks.explanation: A focused function centralizes the rule and lets the same behavior be tested once.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A focused function centralizes the rule and lets the same behavior be tested once.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A focused function centralizes the rule and lets the same behavior be tested once.

blocks.title: Sample 2: Functions and Null Safety in practice
blocks.code:
fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a+b
fun main() { println(add(8,4)) }

blocks.text: Application tip: in a real Kotlin project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.question: A function prints a total but another function needs to calculate with that total. What is usually required?
options: Return the total as a value.
Print the total in a larger font.
Rename the variable only.
Call the function repeatedly until the output is visible.
blocks.explanation: Printing is an output side effect; returning makes the value available to the caller.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Printing is an output side effect; returning makes the value available to the caller.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Printing is an output side effect; returning makes the value available to the caller.

blocks.text: Parameters are the inputs a function accepts; arguments are the actual values supplied by a call. A return value sends a result back to the caller, while printing merely displays information and does not automatically make it available for later calculations.

blocks.question: A function has eight unrelated responsibilities and is hard to test. What is the best improvement?
options: Add more global variables.
Split it into small functions with clear responsibilities.
Remove all function names.
Put all code into one conditional.
blocks.explanation: Small cohesive functions are easier to test and maintain.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Small cohesive functions are easier to test and maintain.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Small cohesive functions are easier to test and maintain.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
Testing a function with normal, minimum, maximum, and invalid inputs exposes assumptions early. Small functions are easier to test and combine than one large function that handles unrelated jobs.

blocks.question: A function receives an unexpected input. What should the contract make clear?
options: Only the function’s color.
The screen size.
How many comments it contains.
Which inputs are valid and what happens for invalid input.
blocks.explanation: A clear function contract specifies assumptions, returned values, and failure behavior.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A clear function contract specifies assumptions, returned values, and failure behavior.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A clear function contract specifies assumptions, returned values, and failure behavior.

blocks.question: A function calculates whether a score passes. How should the caller reuse the result?
options: Infer it from a printed sentence.
Re-run the whole application.
Use the returned Boolean or documented result.
Read the function’s source text at runtime.
blocks.explanation: A returned result is a reliable interface between the function and its caller.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A returned result is a reliable interface between the function and its caller.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A returned result is a reliable interface between the function and its caller.
